question: iq-l1
paraphrase: First I'd see which filesystem has run out of room by listing how much space each mounted volume has left. Then I'd work out which folder is eating it, going level by level and sorting by size, and look for individual huge files, which are usually logs. I would not blindly remove things: I'd figure out what is writing so much and why. To free room I'd compress or truncate old logs, and to stop it happening again I'd set up automatic log rotation and an alert before the volume fills.
wrong: A full disk means the server needs more memory, so I would restart the machine to clear it and then increase the RAM. If that does not help I would reinstall the operating system and ask the hosting provider for a bigger server.

question: iq-k1
paraphrase: You declare what you want, for instance three copies of an app, and the control plane keeps checking what really exists against that. Whenever the two differ, it acts to close the gap. If a container dies, the thing managing the copies starts a replacement. If a whole machine disappears, its workloads get placed on machines that are still healthy.
wrong: Kubernetes heals itself because every pod keeps a backup copy of its data and an administrator gets an email to restart it manually. It mainly relies on Docker Swarm to move virtual machines when the CPU is high.

question: iq-d1
paraphrase: Think of the metal boxes used on cargo ships: whatever is inside, every port and crane can handle them the same way. Docker does that for software. It bundles an application together with everything it needs to run, so it behaves identically on a laptop, a test server and production, and the classic problem of a program running fine for one developer but breaking everywhere else goes away.
wrong: Docker is a programming language made by Google for building websites faster. You write your code in Docker instead of Java and it compiles into a virtual machine that needs its own operating system license.

question: iq-g1
paraphrase: I start from an up-to-date copy of the main line and make a separate line of work for the feature. I save my progress often, each save small and with a message that says what changed. I upload it and ask teammates to look it over through a merge request, fix what they point out, and once it is approved I combine it into the main line as a single tidy change and delete the temporary line of work.
wrong: I work directly on the main branch and commit everything once at the end of the week with the message 'update'. To share it I email the zip file to my team lead and force push if there is a conflict.

question: iq-n1
paraphrase: The name first has to be turned into an address: the browser and operating system look in their caches, otherwise a resolver asks the root servers, the .com servers and finally the site's own name server. With the address the browser opens a reliable connection using the SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange, then negotiates encryption and checks the site's certificate. Over that secure channel it sends a GET and receives the page, and then parses the markup, fetches styles and scripts and paints the result.
wrong: The browser sends the word google.com straight to Google using FTP over port 21, Google looks you up by your MAC address, and the page is downloaded as one image file that the monitor displays.

question: iq-go1
paraphrase: In the first model the build system sits outside the cluster and reaches in to apply changes, so it has to hold powerful cluster keys. In the second, a controller living in the cluster watches the repository and applies whatever changed by itself, so no keys leave the cluster. That controller also keeps comparing the live state with the repository and reverts manual changes.
wrong: Push pipelines are faster because they use HTTP and pull pipelines use FTP. With pull you must log in to every server and run git pull by hand, which is why nobody uses it in production.

question: iq-tf1
paraphrase: Credentials never go into the configuration files or the repository. I feed them in from the shell environment at run time, or have Terraform read them from a dedicated secret store such as HashiCorp's or the cloud provider's. I flag those inputs so they are masked in plan and apply output, and since the state file still contains them in clear text, I keep state in a locked-down bucket with encryption at rest.
wrong: I put the passwords in a variables file and commit it so the whole team has the same values. Terraform encrypts everything in git automatically, and the state file never contains any secrets so it can be shared freely.

question: iq-m1
paraphrase: I begin with the dashboards to see how big the problem is: when it began, which endpoints and what share of users. Then I open slow request traces and see which hop or query takes the time. With a suspect in hand I read that component's log lines from the same minutes for the actual error. Finally I compare with CPU, memory, connection pools and recent deploys to see whether something is exhausted.
wrong: I would restart all the servers one by one until the latency goes away and then clear the browser cache. Observability tools are only needed after an outage for writing the report.

question: iq-sd1
paraphrase: Each long link gets a numeric identifier from a counter, and I write that number using letters and digits so it is short; seven characters cover trillions of links. Lookups are by key only, so a simple key-value database fits. Reads vastly outnumber writes, so I put an in-memory cache in front: check it first, fall back to the database and then populate the cache. For the redirect I choose between a permanent one, which browsers remember, and a temporary one, which lets me count every click.
wrong: I would store every URL in a single text file on one server and search it line by line. The short code is the first six letters of the website name, and I would use a 404 response to send the user to the long address.

question: iq-ci1
paraphrase: Every change goes through a chain of gates. First cheap checks: formatting and static analysis. Then the automated tests, and the run fails if the tested share of the code falls under an agreed minimum. Then I package the app as a container image labelled with the commit hash so any release can be traced. Next the image is tested against real dependencies. Finally it is released to staging and then to a small slice of production traffic, widened only if the metrics stay healthy. The main line is protected so nothing merges without a green run, and the team is told about failures.
wrong: A pipeline is one script that copies files to the server with FTP whenever I remember to run it. Testing is done by customers in production, and I tag every image as latest so I always know which one is running.

question: iq-csh1
paraphrase: Being the superuser inside the container does not mean much when the runtime has stripped its privileges: without them the process cannot attach disks from the host, insert kernel modules or change the clock. A system-call filter adds a second wall by refusing the calls an escape normally needs, such as tracing other processes or loading eBPF programs. So the intruder stays boxed inside that one container.
wrong: Root inside a container is always root on the host, so nothing can stop the attacker. The only protection is a strong password on the container and installing an antivirus inside the image.

question: iq-sre1
paraphrase: I'd first check at the edge whether every instance is slow or only some. Then look at the instances themselves for restarts or crash loops, and read their recent logs for timeouts to the database or to other services. I'd check whether they are out of CPU or memory or being throttled, and whether the database connection pool is exhausted. To stop the bleeding I'd scale out or shed load, and tell stakeholders what is happening.
wrong: A 504 means the customer's internet is slow, so I would wait for the sale to end. If it continues I would delete the pods' persistent volumes and turn off monitoring to save resources.
